Tesla and SpaceX also employ thousands of immigrant engineers, including many on H-1B visas from India and China.

And here’s a simple test: actually listen to Musk’s full interviews instead of reading headlines about them. Whether you agree with him or not, you’ll often find his position is more nuanced than the media portrays. Take the current debate over “remigration.” What he’s consistently emphasized is removing people who are in the country illegally or who commit serious crimes. You can support or oppose that policy, but calling it “racist” skips over the actual argument.

By all means criticize Musk where the facts support it. But judge him by the totality of his actions, his hiring record, and what he actually says in context, not by selectively quoted headlines.

I wish a more complete historical and cultural picture were painted without falling back on the usual B$...  You take the data points of 1936 (Social Security) and today and leave out everything in between.

I am a late boomer, yes I am well off. Why should I be means tested?  I paid more into the Social Security System that I am likely to ever get out.  Despite paying a boatload of property and other taxes, any request for support beyond the basics of police, fire, trash and road maintenance gets met with a hefty fee or "you're on your own, you make too much money." The cutoff for "too much money" is less than my Social Security.   

Peter Drucker wrote about "the succession problem" back in the 1970's, so that is nothing new. It is a simple fact of life that there are far fewer managers than there are workers no matter the era.  

I graduated into the job market in the era of stagflation when the prime rate topped 20% (today ~6%) and mortgage rates topped 16%.  Housing affordability was a joke.  If you were lucky, you rented a place of your own, otherwise you lived in a group home.

I see lots of young people complaining about housing affordability in places like WDC or NYC or LA or SF.  I do not see them clamoring for an affordable house in many smaller towns.  

Yeah, when I started, my life was economically unfair too, but I put my nose to the grindstone and made it.

Balance—not extremes—is where health thrives. As many commenters have pointed out, our healthcare system often focuses more on treating disease than promoting health. Many of the pillars of lifestyle medicine—nutrition, exercise, sleep, stress management, and metabolic health—receive far too little attention during routine care.

Wearable technology can help fill that gap, but only if you're curious and willing to act on the information. If tracking data creates anxiety, a wearable may not be the right tool. But for many people, short-term use of a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) can be eye-opening. I encourage my cancer patients to wear one for 2–4 weeks to discover how simple changes—such as eating vegetables before carbohydrates, taking a walk after meals, or increasing resistant starches—can improve their metabolic health.

Devices like the Oura Ring or WHOOP can also provide valuable insights into sleep, recovery, and heart rate variability (HRV), a useful marker of nervous system resilience. The value comes from observing trends over months, not reacting to a single week's worth of data.

As an integrative cancer care physician, I think of wearables not as gadgets, but as tools that empower patients to better understand their bodies and cultivate a healthier internal terrain.

As a runner, physician and total numbers geek I really like all the data I get from my wearables. I also do use home cortisol testing - not as the company recommends - but as snap shots about my training load. The data has been helpful for me to track and improve my training and has helped me listen to my body - if the numbers are different than how I feel I am pretty good about taking it in stride and just going by how I feel but overall I have gotten good information. 
Having said that, I am NOT a fan of imaging for screening - even with breast cancer, screening did NOT change mortality - just made us overtreat early cancers. It was the improved chemo that changed mortality - new classes of drugs. 
No way would I ever recommend full body imaging. And it would have likely caught my brain tumor earlier but may not have changed treatment - likely it would have been followed until I became symptomatic (which is when we found it).

I am what the mother’s age probably is, and my conservative father’s but also ‘radical’ art-loving mother’s daughter. When my 34-year old married daughter living in Boulder became pregnant (she’d been high risk because of serious endometriosis), I was over the moon. When she started showing, a professional photographer approached her on Pearl Street and invited her to participate in a “Beautiful Mothers of Denver” photoshoot he was putting together for a popular Colorado magazine’s upcoming issue. He promised it would be artistic, minimalist, unapologetic, edgie, and celebrate what modern motherhood looked like in all its raw glory. The only requirement was she had to wear black lingerie. To 95% of the parents on earth, red flags would have screamed from the high heavens — don’t! But to the 5% of us whom understand the power of photography in the right hands — it was a qualified yes. My daughter said, yes. What followed was a whirlwind of connections, trust, and flashing lights. The photoshoot and accompanying article were spectacular and groundbreaking. Over 20 beautiful women, many with their new babies, showed up and donned every manner of black lingerie. The mothers were young, old and grey-haired, some were pregnant, others had had natural births or adopted, one had had a double mastectomy, and several breastfed their babies.

Canada, prior to Mr. Trump's 51st state rhetoric and vicious tariff penalties, accounted for 36% of all US wine exports.  After provincial government and consumer boycotts began in 2025, US wine exports to Canada fell by 78%.  As a result, the Industry estimates a loss of US$ 357 million in one year.  

Canada is unique because most provinces have government-controlled wholesalers.  When Ontario and Quebec, Canada's most populous provinces, removed US imports from their shelves, American wine imports into Canada were reportedly down 90 to 95% compared with the same period a year earlier.

Notably, the boycott was by both governments and consumers.

I said, "What do you think of influencers? What is their job?"

One student piped up, "They inspire!" 

I said, "But we don't call them inspire-ers." 

Another student said, "They motivate!" 

"But we don't call them motivators," I pointed out.

 Blank looks. 

"Think about the word," I said. "INFLUENCers. Now, what do they do?" 

More blank looks. 

I was surprised that they have such a positive, uncritical view of them, and also that they seem to have no idea how the influencer ecosystem works, including what their role as the consumers is. They couldn't even figure out from the wordplay what the verb is in the word "influencer!"

What seems like a simple “soak the rich” idea has much complexity. NYC has a number of days test for tax domicile and one must keep meticulous records of where you were at midnight each day if you want to avoid a tax challenge (although your own records may be challenged). The common law of domicile is different. Domicile once acquired is presumed to continue based on intent and continuation of contacts with your history of domicile. The application of these standards is often abused by the courts where the standard of proof for leaving a high-tax domicile is often higher than than the standard of proof for one unintentionally spending time in the high-tax domicile. 

There is a peculiar Massachusetts case in which someone had a short visit to Boston arriving by plane as they considered maybe moving to Boston. Eventually they did move so the MA could found they acquired a MA domicile as of the time the plane landed. The hook was intention after the fact and the mere nexus of landing in MA was enough. There are other cases where with very similar facts the courts reached very different conclusions. Hindsight becomes foresight. 

So, what will be the criteria for someone with two homes, one in NYC and one elsewhere. Consider if they spent 60% of their time in NYC one year, but only 40% in the next year. A court could rule either way as to the tax domicile for which is the second home. 

For the unwilling taxpayers, the solution is a five-letter word - HOTEL

The antitrust framework feels dangerously quaint when applied to this Paramount Skydance maneuver. We are not merely debating market share or the routine consolidation of movie studios. We are witnessing a calculated ideological capture masquerading as corporate synergy.

Allowing a known Trump supplicant to swallow both CNN and CBS News is a transparent blueprint for constructing a synchronized GOP propaganda apparatus. The rumored elevation of figures like Bari Weiss to enforce ideological conformity across these institutions makes the objective glaringly obvious. The goal is to transform independent journalism into a compliant megaphone for the administration.

When the president uses a White House Correspondents Association dinner to heap praise on preferred executives while gleefully insulting working reporters, the subtext becomes text. The state attorneys general are absolutely right to throw sand in the gears of this acquisition. This fight is not simply about saving Hollywood jobs. It is about preventing the wholesale purchase of the Fourth Estate by a political faction desperate to manufacture its own reality.

comments.name: George S.
comments.body:
Obviously one has to be suspicious of this given it arises from the Trump crowd.

But the reality is that the Federal government is awash with both abandoned and little used land and facilities -- much acquired during both the WWII and Cold War eras.

Depending on location, many of these facilities have (or had) significant utility infrastructure with relatively easy access to the overall power grid.

To the extent that this repurposing can be limited to developed facilities rather than natural land it is an idea worth pursuing.

The reality is that we are entering into a new AI world that will require significant data centers.  Centers that often when proposed in many areas raise serious legitimate public objections.

But to reuse an abandoned military or airbase, for example, substantially lessens the impact compared to prior use.

As we face a "brave new world" determined in large part by AI we have to address the resultant needs.  After all, we can be certain that every nation is facing this same question and no one wants to be left behind.

This article has identified the fundamental problem associated with AI, without identifying it as such.  Every AI system is subject to inputs, and whether it is a government or a private company, bias is impossible to divest.
  This author's call for the government to do something creative is a laughable oxymoron, and ironically mimics what the Chinese government already does—deletes, edits, and inserts. 
   Every day we hear about the dangers of OpenAI.  China is aware of the problem and has derived a solution which jives with its national interests.    

If you want to know about Tiananmen 1989, don't go to DeepSeek; try ChatGPT. If you want to know about Bernie, or Hillary, or Anthony, don't tune in to Fox News, read the NY Times.

   It is not the system that is at fault, but human discernment, which is something that AI does not offer.  China no more wants you to read the US version of Xinjiang, Taiwan, or 1989 than Donald Trump wants you to read the left-wing press about Epstein, Iran, or his criminal activities.  And he is finding ways to suppress it and punish the messengers.

  Everybody's talking about controlling AI.  Watch carefully. Even in the US,  government controls may wind up bending the system to someone's benefit and someone else's disadvantage.
   AI is a wonderful tool. But, like any tool, a buzz-saw ot TNT, know how to handle it and do so with care.

My son is a 1 year old now. Part of our night routine is to say “goodnight” to our house. “Goodnight living room, kitchen, hallway.” “Goodnight Obama, thank you for the hope.” 

When he was tiny he loved the contrasting red/black/blue shades. Now he smiles the biggest smile and reaches his hand out to the poster as we pass. Just yesterday he was standing on the couch next to me and reached over to the bookshelf where I have the book of Obama’s speeches. He started crying real tears reaching for it (he’s never seen it before), so I handed it to him. He opened the front cover and ran his hand gently down the photo of Obama on stage, grinning up at me. I said “that’s Obama who gives us hope”. He studied the photo so hard then smiled again. 

What does it say that a 2 min campaign video watching these two shoot hoops breathes more life into my household than an entire State of the Union address from Trump? 

Thank you for the hope, Obama, always.

comments.name: David Jaspen
comments.body: The current system is really the best compromise, even if people don’t like the twice-yearly clock changing. Year-round daylight saving time is impractical because of excessively late sunrises in the late fall and early winter. Year-round standard time would deprive us of gloriously late sunsets and “waste” early morning sunshine when few would be awake to enjoy it.

comments.name: Paul B
comments.body:
Growing up in Upstate NY, I experienced many years of short days when it was getting dark not long after I got home from school and it was just barely dawn before I was off to school again. Big deal…

It is “more honest” to me to keep Standard Time year round. The statement that, “Some people think that the time is just a random number we pull out of the sky, but it is, in fact, a specific number that we measure out of the sky.” says it perfectly.

comments.name: ShiningLight
comments.body:
Regarding religion and clocks - a memory from the 1960's - meeting my soon to be grandmother-in-law, for the first time mid-summer 1960's, I quietly mentioned to my fiance that her kitchen clock was an hour slow.  She heard me, and I was told that it was set to "God's Time" year round.   :-)

A Christian, she was born in 1885 and saw things go from Queen Victoria's days to Man Landing on the Moon - quite a lot of changes and didn't like anyone monkeying around with what time it was.  In her beloved memory we keep a clock set on EST year round.

These days I would like to see clocks set to DST year round. - Sorry Grandma Thomas ---

comments.name: Charlie Hall
comments.body: I am an Orthodox Jew and I am appalled by the reason for the opposition. Having the Sabbath start at 530pm rather than 430pm in the winter will make life much Much MUCH easier for Sabbath-observamt Jews and for Jews who would like to observe the Sabbath but can't leave their jobs early. Observing the Sabbath is much Much MUCH more important than attending morning services in synagogue.

And I was lucky that I didn't have to walk to school or cross any busy streets, and that my neighborhood had sidewalks.  I also lived in Virginia, so it wasn't that cold, compared to where I live now, where it can be extremely cold and icy in winter.  And that neighborhood was generally safer than the one I live in now.  I would not want my own child walking to school in the dark at any age. Children and youth already have a hard time getting up that early and will suffer yet more sleep deprivation.  I'd prefer the status quo or year-around standard time.

I like more daylight hours when I'm off work, not when I'm at work. I remember as a kid in NYC the winter we had daylight savings time in effect and I was out walking to the bus before dawn in the dark for at the most two weeks.  It felt special and the one morning it started to snow was an incredibly magical experience which I have never forgotten. I still treasure the memory of that morning. I also don't remember anybody dying but NYC kids are raised to be street smart even before dawn.

Around the globe, city managers and politicians need to understand that we have entered a century of fire.

ALL communities with any significant greenery will eventually need to deal with wildfires because the entire planet is getting warmer.

Here in the U.S., too many people think that massive wildfires are only a thing in the western U.S. which traditionally had a wildfire season of several months each year.

But the western U.S. now has a wildfire season for the entire year--and the rest of the U.S. will soon have their own wildfire seasons.

Today, it is Oregon, Utah, New Mexico, and California, but eventually it will be Maine, Upstate New York, Virginia, North Carolina and more.

Many places in the U.S. aren’t prepared for California-style wildfires. But these fires are on the way.

Each year will have a hotter average temperature than the last.  Maybe scientists should model when each state can expect to see the start of mega-wildfires based on when local temperatures are predicted to increase to a level that no longer suits existing vegetation.

Eventually, the forest fires will give way to bush fires, the bush fires will give way to grass fires, and finally we’ll see an end to mega-fire season because we will have dust storms instead.

On our journey from a blue-green Earth to a dust-red Earth, if human society is to survive in some form, we must be honest about what is happening—and come up with plans—instead of ignoring what should be obvious to all.

comments.body: Love is love- acceptance is love.  Love your daughter enough to be brave to let your Mom know that she has a granddaughter not a grandson.  If she is upset - oh well that is her choice to be. If she cuts you off - oh well that is her choice to do so- but that is not love.  Do not let someone’s opinion - anyone’s opinion steal your joy and steal your daughter’s joy. Love is love.

comments.name: Claudia
comments.body:
"Ultimately, the goal here isn’t to force your family into ideological agreement. It’s to end a pattern of erasing parts of yourself and violating your integrity by making secrecy the price of belonging."

sometimes i feel angry and resentful for being raised  amidst such conservative surroundings and people, and i find myself now browbeating my folks with my progressive ideologies, rather than giving them generous amounts of space to navigate their own paths. this resonates.

comments.name: Sarah B
comments.body: Excellent advice.

comments.name: Eliz
comments.body:
"Willing to be out" but not interested in visiting doesn't sound like a ringing endorsement of the letter writer's daughter feeling connected to their mother's concerns.

As a parent of a trans adult child I am -like other commenters- confused about why the grandchild isn't in charge of this whole decision making process. It is hard to glean how supportive the letter writer was of their child at the outset though clearly they love and support their child. Maybe if the writer's mother is coming to visit the best thing is to reach back to the daughter and ask what they might envision themselves in terms of what steps they see to sharing this news. The letter writer's daughter has already experienced many reactions from their community about their transition and has their own relationship with their grandparent.
In our experience supporting our daughter at each step from behind as they made the choices about when and how to work with family- or any- relationship coming out was with with total support and love from our end based in us trusting that she was in charge of her path. However the news is shared or what the reaction that comes is the letter writer can show clearly that they are there for their daughter.

comments.name: Andante
comments.body:
Lori nailed it. All of it.

I feel so bad for all the people who struggle with this situation. I didn’t tell my mom quite a few things (including that my guardian had tried to molest me while she was overseas) to protect her feelings as well as mine, and I’d happily do it again—but in this case it’s an ongoing, frequent, uncomfortable lie. And if grandma does come to visit, she’s gonna find out the truth.

Better to tell her now, so that she can absorb this and come to terms with it before any visit. 

Better still, OP’s daughter might want to write grandma a letter, both because it’s HER story to tell and because she’s the one who can best explain why.

comments.name: Maggie
comments.body:
The daughter has never seen the grandmother and doesn’t especially wish to. Therefore it doesn’t matter whether GM knows or not. GM’s approval and support are not valued.

The grandmother is 90. It’s a rare person at that age who can upend all their previous views. It would upset her and cause conflict which she might not live long enough to become reconciled to. 

Here’s a better plan. When asked about your child just reply about other parts of her life: a new job, bought a house, told a funny joke.

comments.name: CT
comments.body: The granddaughter has no relationship with the family (they don’t even know she is a woman).  I worry the family is going to harshly judge her as they would any other trans stranger. They sound like close-minded, stress-inducing terrible people. I wouldn’t trust them to be loving and accepting. Why subject the granddaughter to that?

articles.title: Should I Tell My Conservative Mom Her Grandchild Is Trans?

comments.name: TokyoExpat

comments.name: RAnnBrunIsDumb

comments.name: A need for change

comments.body:
Really, a remarkable building and a great legacy for Hadid.

I clicked over to the official site to see more photos (and also did a quick image search). While I get it that most architectural photography doesn’t include people, in this case it would have enhanced the images to see the scale of them in contrast to the building.

For example, I was wondering about elevators, and one of the official photos shows them tucked under a swooping balcony. And they look tiny in comparison to the scale of the place, which gave me a sense of its true size. 

How much better would architecture be served to show how it appears and performs with its intended users: human beings?

comments.name: Sara
comments.body: A day after an article about the opening of the long-delayed Guggenheim Abu-Dhabi by Frank Gehry, this article about Zaha Hadid's Royal Theater of Rabat. Titans both. But as time goes by, I think Hadid's work will be seen to be the more important, the more interesting. Increasingly to me, at least, Gehry's forms have come to seem fussy, silly rather than playful, eye-popping for no other reason to be eye-popping, like a lot of art and design from the 1980s and 90s. Hadid's on the other hand have gravitas. The forms seem genuinely organic and necessary. Startling, too, but not in a fun house way. Her buildings are genuinely strange, genuinely thought-provoking. Dramatic and grand and dignified. Gehry's amuse. But I tire of them far more quickly.

comments.name: Michael Turkic
comments.body: An amazing building no doubt. I have been inside the Guangzhou houses (there are two, one white one black) like two pebbles side by side. They are remarkable by any stretch of anyone's imagination. However on closer inspection inside both the public common areas and the performance spaces, you can see the lack of craftsmanship in fixtures and fittings. Premature cracking on the facades on the inside walls, rust spots coming through, flakes of paint chipping off. Our guide just brushed past all this in an effort to divert attention. What a shame Ms Hadid had to endure this type of shoddy construction, but, as we all know, China is famous for making things look great on the outside but the real side is not as forgiving.

comments.name: David Gardiner
comments.body: Regarding Cuba: Wouldn’t it be better to establish friendly relations with that country instead of considering it our enemy? We could tell them that we plan to remove our occupation of their territory with our military base/prison at Guantanamo. We could suspend all sanctions and blockades and at the same time offer some financial assistance to help them get their beleaguered economy going. We could open up some trade avenues with them. I think the government there would respond positively to such actions. This might sound utopian to many but it is eminently practical. I think we would see that country immediately begin to open up and evolve into a freer and more democratic system.

comments.body: Thoughtful response to climate creep.  In the past five years, armadillos have made it into the foothills of the Appalachian mountains in east Tennessee.  I'm hoping water moccasins don't follow suit.  And the insect population has declined precipitously here.  Butterflies, since pre-covid, have become singular rather than profuse, even amidst the long time presence of native pollinating plants.  Down in the valley, snapping turtles don't come up the creek to spawn any more.  Frog eggs have disappeared where they used to be profuse.  Fifteen years ago I broke my arm scrambling over slimy rocks to count 8 or so  pairs of wood frogs mating.  There's a litany of anecdotal evidence one can observe. Perhaps the increasing silence in the spring and on warm summer nights will wake us up to the future we are creating.

comments.name: Guillaume
comments.body:
This is the landscape of my childhood: the Atlantic coast, the pine forests, the places where I still visit my parents. I was there only a few weeks ago. Watching it burn from California is heartbreaking because this is not some distant disaster. This is home going up in flames.

My family is safe today. In 2022, the fires came considerably closer. But thousands of people have now fled their homes, others have lost them entirely, and firefighters and local residents are again being asked to confront conditions that grow more dangerous each summer.

Fires are not new, and climate change does not strike every match. But extreme heat, prolonged drought and high winds increasingly determine what happens after the match is struck. Containment is therefore an enormous relief, but it is not resolution. The summer is far from over, and another heat wave is already arriving.

We should be profoundly grateful to the firefighters and citizens confronting the immediate emergency. But gratitude cannot substitute for political action. We have understood the larger trajectory for years. What remains astonishing is that governments are still constrained by denial, partisan deadlock and half-measures while cherished landscapes, homes and communities burn.

Couple this with the fact that the eastern half of the province of Inner Mongolia borders China "bread basket" provinces of Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang which produce the majority of China's corn, soybeans and other feed products.  Northeast China also sits on the Pacific Ocean and has the excellent port of Dalian.  I can definitely see the region moving ahead in the next 5-10 years to not only ship high quality beef to Shanghai and the major cities up and down China's coast but also moving product out to South Korea and Japan.  

In the meanwhile, President Trump and the Republican Congress have been actively dismantling and downsizing our US Department of Agriculture through laying off 20% of employees, closing market programs, relocating data analysis, domestic and foreign policy agencies to remote parts of Maryland and Kansas, and making it more difficult for our farmers to export because of inflationary tariff wars.

Of course it is China's goal to control the stack. Before I retired I worked on Ethernet standards for several different companies (Fujitsu, Cisco, and Huawei). Here's how it works. Your company patents its technology and then proposes that this technology becomes part of the standard. Then you trade patent rights with other companies. Cisco was the best at doing this. But, now China is doing this... and they are accused of controlling the stack. Give me a break... this is just more China-bashing.

If China wants to maintain domestic control, they will simply require that Chinese companies modify the open source accordingly. People don't have to run open source unmodified.

I believe China is heading into a long economic downward trend for a number of reasons.  First, demographics points to an aging population with the affects of the one child policy hampering a traditional population replacement.  That's a demand issue. 

Second, lack of social programs in Healthcare and pensions means consumers have less disposable income to spend versus savings. Again, a demand issue. 

Third, plainly the production machine China has perfected has developed produced plants now operating below capacity, coupled with trading partners lagging economies and their own demographic issues with lower birth rates.  These lead to excess inventories for producers. China can no longer count on exports as their main driver for growth -- they need to develop a strong consumer segment, and that will come with higher costs of production which will affect China's price advantages with its trading partners.

Like their massive container ships, it will take a long time to turn their economy around and I predict the middle powers/countries will have an advantage as they are already more nimble to make changes in their economies as they unwind from China's dominance.

In the US, we see increasing number of people without health insurance (see https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/30/business/aca-obamacare-health-insurance.html from today's paper). In China, there is universal healthcare.

In China, when the government sees problems like unemployment or an increasing income divide, it works to address them. In the US, we have a congress that does nothing but embarrass itself with performances like yesterday's Fauci hearing.

Let's stop worrying so much about China... they're doing fine. Let's worry more about us.

This article is quite focused on what I see as relatively short-term issues. Chinese planners look at problems with a horizon of years. They will maintain the strength of their exports, while gradually building domestic spending. They are not going to view this as an immediate crisis. 

The US, on the other hand, doesn't plan one day ahead (with the exception of the Fed, one of our institutions that still words).

In my 30+ years of teaching dramatic literature (courses in which we read plays as literature), I've selected "Ma Rainey's Black Bottom" more than "Fences," "The Piano Lesson," or any other Wilson play. Not sure why; I just like it better than those two and other Wilson plays.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
We are already seeing increases in wildfire intensity. At a 2.0°C rise, wildfires will intensify non-linearly due to exponential increases in Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD). Warm air holds roughly 7% more moisture per degree Celsius, aggressively drying forest canopies, soil duff, and high-elevation vegetation that once acted as natural firebreaks. Models project a doubling to quadrupling of annual burned area across Western North America and Boreal regions compared to late 20th-century baselines, along with up to a 100% increase in burned area across the Mediterranean.

This warming also expands fire seasons globally, causing Northern and Southern Hemisphere peak windows to overlap and strain firefighting resources. Higher fuel dryness triggers more frequent pyrocumulonimbus events—firestorms that generate dry lightning and spot fires miles ahead of the main front. Large high-severity burn patches will increasingly prevent natural forest recovery, risking permanent conversions to shrubland while releasing massive stores of soil carbon back into the atmosphere.

Those are some of the sights and sounds of the beginning of dramatic climate changes coming.

There were numerous times when I asked AI to check its responses because I spotted an error with its claim about what materials said, and when AI said that it checked its answers without actually doing so. When I confronted it with quotes from material and asked what happened, it gave me a guess that it relied on its interpretation of the source instead of the source- which I explicitly told it not to do.

AI does not lie like people do. When people lie, they get vague, they don’t cite, and there are tells that they are lying. AI does not have the same tells.

However AI “thinks,” it does not “think” like people do. There are advantages that AI has, certainly, like its speed in processing large amount of info, but there are also downsides. I suspect one of the biggest downsides is our inability to understand it.

So the regulations for AI may need to focus on incentivizing and protecting whistleblowers for AI. People who probably have a better shot at understanding how AI “thinks” then rest of us.

Our daily temperatures have been consistently about 25-27 degrees Celsius with a constant breeze from the Atlantic. Idyllic. We have had one spate of days over 30 but that seems like a vague memory, as the forecasts call for more of the current weather for the next many days well into August. 

I say all this not to boast at my luck of having fallen upon utopic summer weather but to say how easy it is to feel like the climate crisis is not an urgent issue when, in fact it is. I say this also to shed light on how easily we can fall back into complacency after the immediate threat is over.  Indeed, I seem to have forgotten the devastating series of named storms this winter right here in the Oeste region of Portugal where I live. We endured what seemed like interminable rain and flooding. Roads were washed out. Driving, we couldn’t get to town from our village because the river crossed over the main roads. Many roads remain closed months later. We were without running water for 2 1/2 weeks as the  pipes burst and the deluge undid the water company’s repair efforts. People in some municipalities were without power for three months. Most importantly, lives and property were destroyed.  These storms were unprecedented and most assuredly because of our changing climate.

Yet, I seem to forget all that in this Western Portuguese summer.

Making Daylight Saving Time permanent year-round is a bad idea because it would force much of the country to endure extremely late winter sunrises. The inflection year point for Big Law is extraordinarily easy to chronicle accurately: 1986, with the first tremors in the immediately preceding years.

That's the very year that large law firm compensation schemes and structures were significantly overhauled, first in Manhattan and very quickly spreading to Chicago, LA, SFO, DC, Philly & Boston, among others. Old partnerships got three-tiered: Of-counsel, (full) partner, junior partner. Associate salary tiers got bumped by 20%, but billable hour expectations got bumped by 25%. It was the year many younger lawyers in Big Law saw the churn coming in their direction, and that far fewer would make full partner; as a result, many of them made decisions about where to set their workplace boundaries, with a cold calculus about the likely consequences of decisions. But there is another side to HPV related cancers that remains underfunded and with no screening recommendations at all. Anal cancer kills >2000 year and there is no recommended screening. But by far the biggest killer of HPV related cancers is Head and Neck cancers, killing between 11,000 and 12,000 annually, the vast majority of them men. Boys still lag significantly in receiving the HPV vaccine, despite it being recommended for boys starting in 2011. The marketing and public perception is that the vaccine is for "cervical cancer" a great disservice to boys, who have have a greater risk of dying from head and neck cancer then women do of cervical cancer, and would benefit more directly from the vaccine. We need equal, or even greater research into the early detection of head and neck cancers, since they are killing more people, particularly men. We need to stop thinking HPV = cervical cancer. HPV causes mucosal cancers, and throat cancer actually kills far more men in the USA than women from cervical. Parents, vaccinate your boys too, anyone who has an anus, penis, cervix or throat needs it!
